recent_posts.title: Neovim 0.12 setup for config editing, markdown writing, and system utilities
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of a revamped Neovim setup built for Neovim 0.12, covering three main use cases: inserting screenshots into markdown articles via a custom hotkey, yanking UUIDs from system files like fstab on headless servers, and using an integrated LLM for single-file code analysis. The setup moves away from kickstart toward a more minimal config, using plugins like snacks for file picking and live grep, oil for file navigation, and a tab system for multi-project work. The author also compares Neovim to VS Code and Cursor, noting Neovim's strengths in fast editing and config work but acknowledging VS Code and Cursor remain superior for AI agent-assisted coding on large projects.

Bazzite vs CachyOS vs Linux Mint for new users switching from Windows
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide comparing three Linux distributions for Windows users switching to Linux: Bazzite (for gamers who want things to work out of the box), CachyOS (for power users wanting an Arch-based system with flexibility), and Linux Mint (for office/basic users wanting stability). Covers installation steps for each, key features like atomic updates in Bazzite, desktop environment choices in CachyOS, and the beginner-friendly update manager in Mint. Also touches on Distrobox, Topgrade, Flatpak, and gaming compatibility caveats on Linux.

recent_posts.title: Why Pop OS with Cosmic desktop is not ready for new Linux users
recent_posts.summary: Pop!OS with the Cosmic desktop environment is criticized as unsuitable for new Linux users in 2026. The Cosmic DE is still in beta/alpha stages yet ships as the default in Pop!OS 24 LTS, which contradicts the stability promise of an LTS release. Key issues include significant memory leaks (Cosmic launcher consuming up to 17GB RAM), GPU/display driver bugs, audio problems, and over 1,700 unaddressed GitHub issues with little community engagement from System76. The author recommends Linux Mint for stability-focused users, Bazzite for gamers, and CachyOS for power users instead.

recent_posts.title: Basic network security practices every home user should follow
recent_posts.summary: A beginner-friendly overview of basic network security practices for home users. Covers scanning external ports with GRC ShieldsUP, inspecting active connections and listening ports using TCPView on Windows and ss/netstat/lsof on Linux, reducing attack surface by disabling SSH/VNC/RDP when not needed, choosing better routers (Ubiquiti UniFi or pfSense over ISP-provided hardware), configuring software firewalls (UFW on Linux, Windows Firewall or SimpleWall on Windows), and debunking VPN myths while clarifying their actual use cases. Emphasizes that security is an ongoing process, not a one-time fix.

recent_posts.title: Exploiting unpatched Windows 10 is harder than you think
recent_posts.summary: A sysadmin with 25 years of experience revisits his earlier warnings about Windows 10 end-of-life security risks. After attempting to exploit an unpatched Windows 10 1607 instance using Metasploit and the EternalBlue/DoublePulsar exploit, he found it surprisingly difficult — largely because a secure, business-grade network with deep packet inspection blocked the attacks even when the OS firewall was disabled. He softens his previous stance: while updating is still recommended, unpatched Windows 10 is not as immediately exploitable as commonly feared, especially on a secure network. He recommends Windows 10 LTSC for legacy use cases and encourages users who dislike Windows 11 to consider switching to Linux.

recent_posts.title: Windows 10 end of life what you should do now
recent_posts.summary: Windows 10 reached end of life on October 14, 2025, meaning no more security updates for Home and Pro users. Nearly half of surveyed users are still on Windows 10, which poses real security risks as unpatched systems become easy targets. Options include upgrading to Windows 11 (using tools like Win 11 Creator for a clean install), switching to LTSC for a short-term extension, paying for Extended Security Updates (ESU), or migrating to Mac or Linux. Feature updates are optional but security updates are non-negotiable for staying protected.
